payload.explanation_text:
A cell membrane surrounds the cell. It controls what moves in and out.

The membrane is built from phospholipids. Each phospholipid has two parts. The head likes water. The tails avoid water. A molecule with both kinds of parts is called amphipathic. In water, the heads face outward and the tails hide inside. This forms a double layer called a bilayer. Each layer is a leaflet.

The tails are fatty acids. A fatty acid is a chain of carbon atoms. Saturated tails have no double bonds. Their straight shape lets them pack tightly. Unsaturated tails have double bonds. Each double bond creates a bend. These bends make tight packing harder. This allows more movement. Fluidity means how freely membrane parts move.

Several things affect fluidity. These include saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol.

Cholesterol acts as a buffer. When the membrane is too fluid, cholesterol restrains excess movement. When it is cold, cholesterol helps keep the membrane from stiffening.

The fluid mosaic model describes this structure. The membrane is a mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins. These parts can move sideways.

The two leaflets contain different mixtures of molecules. Lipids rarely switch leaflets on their own. Special enzymes help them move. These enzymes include flippases, floppases, and scramblases.

Sugar chains on the outer surface form the glycocalyx, or sugar coating. The glycocalyx helps cells recognize each other. It also helps a cell tell self from non-self.

concepts.name: Amphipathic phospholipids form the bilayer
concepts.taught_summary: Phospholipids have a water-loving head and water-avoiding tails. In water, the heads face outward and the tails face inward, forming a bilayer made of two leaflets.

concepts.name: Saturated vs. unsaturated fatty acids
concepts.taught_summary: Saturated tails have no double bonds and pack tightly. Double bonds in unsaturated tails create bends that make tight packing harder and allow more movement.

concepts.name: What affects membrane fluidity
concepts.taught_summary: Fluidity is how freely membrane parts move. Saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol affect fluidity.

concepts.name: Cholesterol as a fluidity buffer
concepts.taught_summary: Cholesterol restrains excess movement when the membrane is too fluid. It also helps keep the membrane from stiffening when it is cold.

concepts.name: Fluid mosaic model
concepts.taught_summary: The membrane is a mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins. These components can move sideways.

concepts.name: Membrane asymmetry and lipid flipping
concepts.taught_summary: The two leaflets contain different mixtures of molecules. Lipids rarely switch leaflets without help from enzymes such as flippases, floppases, and scramblases.

concepts.name: Glycocalyx and cell recognition
concepts.taught_summary: Sugar chains on the outer surface form the glycocalyx. It helps cells recognize each other and tell self from non-self.
